clinicalPearls: End-organ resistance to parathyroid hormone, predominantly in the renal proximal tubule, caused by loss of methylation at the maternal GNAS locus that reduces expression of the stimulatory G-protein alpha subunit (Gsalpha).
Biochemistry mimics hypoparathyroidism — hypocalcaemia with hyperphosphataemia — but the parathyroid hormone level is elevated, reflecting resistance rather than deficiency.

Unlike type 1A, affected individuals typically lack the Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype, having normal stature without brachydactyly or ectopic ossification, and normal Gsalpha activity in blood cells.
Many have mild resistance to thyroid-stimulating hormone (a subclinical hypothyroid picture) because the thyroid also shows partial paternal imprinting of GNAS.
The autosomal dominant familial form is caused by maternally inherited STX16 microdeletions that produce isolated loss of methylation at the GNAS A/B differentially methylated region.
Sporadic cases usually show broader GNAS methylation defects, sometimes arising from paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 20q.
Because the locus is imprinted, the biochemical disease manifests only when the defect is carried on or arises on the maternal allele.
Presentation is typically with hypocalcaemic symptoms such as paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm, tetany or seizures.
reference.pathophysiology: GNAS on chromosome 20q13 is a complex imprinted locus encoding the stimulatory G-protein alpha subunit (Gsalpha). Gsalpha is expressed from both alleles in most tissues, but predominantly from the maternal allele in a few — notably the renal proximal tubule, thyroid, gonad and pituitary — because of tissue-specific imprinting. In pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B the normal maternal methylation pattern at the GNAS differentially methylated regions (particularly the A/B region) is lost, silencing maternal Gsalpha expression in these tissues; the proximal tubule then cannot mount an adequate cAMP response to parathyroid hormone, producing PTH resistance with hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia and a compensatory rise in PTH. The familial autosomal dominant form arises from maternally transmitted deletions in the neighbouring STX16 gene that remove a cis-acting control element and cause isolated A/B loss of methylation, whereas sporadic disease shows broader GNAS methylation abnormalities or paternal uniparental disomy of 20q. Because Gsalpha activity in blood cells is generally preserved, erythrocyte Gsalpha is normal, contrasting with type 1A.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (GNAS coding mutation with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy and multi-hormone resistance)
Primary hypoparathyroidism (with a low parathyroid hormone)
Vitamin D deficiency or hereditary vitamin D resistance
Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism (Albright features with normal biochemistry, paternal transmission)
Chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism
additionalInvestigations: Corrected or ionised calcium, phosphate and magnesium
Intact parathyroid hormone (elevated in the context of hypocalcaemia)
Thyroid function tests to screen for TSH resistance
GNAS methylation analysis (for example methylation-specific MLPA) of the differentially methylated regions
STX16 deletion testing and, where indicated, testing for uniparental disomy of chromosome 20q
Electrocardiogram for hypocalcaemia and brain imaging for basal ganglia calcification
redFlags: Prolonged QT interval or arrhythmia related to hypocalcaemia
Symptomatic hypothyroidism from unrecognised TSH resistance
New neurological symptoms with basal ganglia calcification
reference.prognosis: The outlook is good with lifelong oral calcium and an active vitamin D analogue together with monitoring of calcium and renal status; because Albright hereditary osteodystrophy is absent, stature and skeletal development are typically normal, although TSH resistance may require thyroid hormone replacement.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the condition as primary hypoparathyroidism, when the parathyroid hormone is high rather than low.
Assuming that the absence of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy excludes pseudohypoparathyroidism, since these features are characteristically absent in type 1B.
Failing to screen for TSH resistance and thereby missing treatable hypothyroidism.
Relying on routine karyotype or coding-sequence analysis, which are normal — methylation-specific testing is required for diagnosis.
Forgetting the imprinting rule, so that only maternal transmission of the defect produces the biochemical disease.

Monitor calcium, phosphate, PTH, renal function and urinary calcium to avoid hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis
